title: How much of an open-source chip design search can cheap fidelity rungs and proof prediction save, with a guarantee?
lede: an honest, mostly negative multi-fidelity study on real SKY130 place-and-route: cheap rungs mis-rank routed area x delay (generic-gate tau-b median -0.04), successive halving does not beat random routed search, and proof success is predicted by design size rather than by the rewrite; a theorem bounds halving's regret by the cut rungs' inversions, and a pilot with ratio below 1 certifies that halving returns a cost no worse than the pilot's best point (0 violations in 1.5 million draws), a ceiling about 2.7 times the realised regret; on a fresh 120-sequence pool the held-out schedule 'skip the generic-gate rung, keep 8' has 1.04% routed regret against 5.49% for the hand-chosen one, a gap made by one tie-heavy design. On 26 held-out designs it beats random routing of the same wall-clock where routing costs over 3 times a mapped score (2.07% against 3.59% regret) and loses where routing is cheap; a rule fixed before any routing (ladder only above a 3x cost ratio, else random) halves the regret of either policy on held-out designs (1.66% against 2.29% and 4.38%). on eight designs no table had run (milestone 113) the rule has 0.91% regret against 2.64% for random routing and 1.44% for always running the ladder. a mapped score clipped at the clock period (milestone 115) cuts that rule's regret on seven new designs, run blind, from 2.73% to 0.83%. Counted by what each rule had seen (milestone 117), the clipped switch has 1.60% regret against 2.91% for equal-cost random routing on the 24 cells of 12 designs run after its parameters were fixed (better in 18, worse in 5), while the switch without the clip is level with random routing on designs it had not seen. A further blind test on three new families (milestone 118) refutes a general win: a 128-bit funnel shifter, whose mapped delay carries no routed-delay information, costs the rule 39 to 51%, so over its 36 test cells it has 3.85% against 2.77% for random routing, and 0.79% against 2.59% once shifter families are excluded after the fact. Two structural guards were then tested blind (milestones 119 and 120). Checking the RTL for a shift operator misses a barrel built from muxes (18 to 20% against 2 to 3% random) and wrongly flags a leading-zero normaliser, where the ladder reaches 0.00%. A third blind test (milestone 121) puts the line by where the shift amount comes from: a popcount-driven shifter is where the ladder wins (0.00% in all 4 cells), while one adder or an exponent difference in front of the amount still leaves the ladder losing; a guard that routes randomly on shifters whose amount is under 8 word-level cells deep has 2.89% against 3.34% for random routing (better in 4 cells, worse in none). Two more blind tests place the line by the logic in gates, not in word-level cells (milestones 122 and 123): on six shifters built so the two counts disagree, a guard that routes randomly when fewer than 36 gates feed the shift amount has 1.28% regret against 5.33% for the word-level guard and 3.95% for random routing (better than random in 7 cells, worse in 1), and over the 36 blind cells of milestones 121 to 123 it has 2.25% against 3.94% (better in 17, worse in 1). A seventh blind test (milestone 124, seven shifters with 31 to 41 gates in front of the amount) puts the cut between 31 and 33 gates, below the registered 36: the ladder wins on every cell from 33 gates up, so the 36-gate guard is too cautious (2.84% blind regret, against 1.38% at 32 or 33 and 8.11% for random routing) but still never worse than random. An eighth blind test (milestone 125, eight shifters from four new families) refutes gate depth as the separating variable: the ladder wins at 28 to 35 gates and loses at 36 on a multiplier-driven amount, so the 32-gate guard does worse than no guard (6.79% against 3.56%, random 5.69%), while 64-bit multi-lane shifters reach the ladder branch and the ladder wins there. A probe-rank guard on random points (milestone 126, replay) does not help either (5.14% against 4.77% unguarded and 5.44% random): the mapped score's overall order is as good where the ladder fails, and it goes wrong only among its own top-ranked points. A top-probe guard (milestone 127, replay) routes the ladder's own best 3 points against 3 random ones and does detect a failing cell (54% of draws, against 7% false alarms), but with the whole pool already mapped the fall-back is too small, so it lands at 5.11%. A staged version (milestone 128, replay) makes the same check on a random 24-point subset before mapping the rest, so a distrusting draw keeps its budget: it cuts the failing cells' regret from 16.63% to 9.16%, but its probes cost 4.23 points where the ladder was perfect, so it lands at 5.31%. A pilot-probe version (milestone 129, replay) tests the subset's best point against the one random point the rule already routes to time the flow, so a trusting draw almost always routes the same 8 points as no guard: it is the first measured guard below the unguarded ladder (4.39% against 4.77%, random 5.44%), though it is worse on more cells than it is better and stays behind the 32-gate rule (3.91%). Hedging its fall-back with the subset's next ranks (milestone 130) is nearly free and nearly useless (4.37%): the false alarms come from the test, not the fall-back. Confirming an alarm with a second random probe before falling back (milestone 131) cuts false alarms threefold (12% to 4% of draws) but misses most true ones (34% to 14%), so it is worse on the mean (4.53%) though better on more cells (47 to 20): a second random point barely tells a failing ranking from a good one. Tested blind with a flow run on six new shifters (milestone 132), neither the pilot-probe guard (3.01%) nor the 32-gate rule (2.25%) beats random routing (2.20%): the ladder fails at 24 gates, where the rule catches it, and at 51 gates on a substitution-table amount, where it does not, and the pilot test sees both failures (distrust 0.31 against 0.04) but its fall-back recovers only part of the loss. Milestones 1 to 132 are in the log
summary: An open research programme with milestones 1 to 97 logged; milestone 1 is described first, later milestones follow, and the log in the project README has the rest. Over 10 small designs, 60 ABC pass sequences each and two clock targets (1,200 runs through Yosys, ABC and OpenROAD on SKY130 HD), the generic-gate rung's Kendall tau-b against routed (global-route plus timing repair) area × period is below 0.7 on all 9 designs where it is defined (median −0.04), and its pick costs a median 13.5% of routed area × period. The liberty-mapped rung is no better than 0.59 median tau at a tight clock (median regret 10.5%) but nearly exact at a relaxed one (0% regret), because timing repair reorders designs. Routed points cost about 8× a generic point here, so there is little to save on designs this small. Limits: one corner and utilisation, global-route estimates, ten small designs. Milestone 2 replays search on the cached table at equal wall-clock: screening the pool at the generic-gate or mapped rung and verifying the top points does not beat random or hill-climbing search (45 s: regret 1.08% and 1.27% against 0.94% and 0.61%), and loses badly at smaller budgets. Hypotheses H2 to H5 (multi-fidelity wins, coverage, proof prediction) are not yet run. Milestone 3 replays successive halving across the four rungs: starting from the generic-gate rung it is the worst strategy (about 10% mean routed regret at the tight clock at 45 s against 0.94% for random search); starting at the mapped rung wins on most designs at a relaxed clock but loses heavily on two; a 6-point routed pilot that picks the start rung recovers the designs plain halving loses (H3), so there is no multi-fidelity gain at equal wall-clock on this 50-point pool yet. Milestone 4 (H4) replays conformal shortlists: a routed pilot of 10 to 16 points calibrates a one-sided bound on routed area × delay from a cheap rung. On the mapped rung the routed optimum is kept 0.99 of the time at nominal 0.90 (0.90–0.92 at 0.80) while routing 42–57% of the pool, against 0.53–0.65 for random search with equal routed runs; on the generic-gate rung coverage is 0.65 at nominal 0.80, no better than random search, so H4 is refuted there. Limits: 20 groups from 10 small designs, one corner. H5 (milestone 5): across 752 Yosys SAT-miter proofs of ABC rewrites on 15 designs, proof time is set by design size (multiplier median 0.01 s at 4 bits, 11 s at 8, over 10 s at 9–10) and never by a rewrite failing; leave-one-design-out AUC is high pooled (0.96–0.998) only because it reads design size, and within the 8-bit multiplier it is 0.65–0.78 against 0.81 for the rule “the rewrite shrinks the netlist”. One solver, one timeout. Milestone 6 (theory): define a rung’s inversion as the largest log-factor by which it ranks a truly worse candidate at or ahead of a better one; halving’s routed regret is then at most the sum of the cut rungs’ inversions (proved; holds on all 40 table cells). It is vacuous for the generic-gate rung (inversion above 0.3 on 8 of 10 groups) and loose for the mapped rungs (bound 0.23–0.35 against about 0 realised); a 10-point pilot sees a median 52–67% of the inversion but cannot certify it. The probabilistic version is open. Milestone 133 (blind, flow run): on seven new 128-bit left shifters chosen by a routing-cost probe so every cell reaches the ladder branch, the unguarded clipped ladder has 2.70% mean regret against 5.57% for equal-cost random routing, and both guards found on seen cells lose to it (gate-depth rule 3.09%, pilot probe 3.35%); pooled over all 42 blind cells the ladder has 3.30% against 4.65% random (better on 28 cells, worse on 8). Milestone 136 (blind-evaluation table): scored only on the cells that were out of sample for each rule, no guard beats the unguarded ladder after a Holm correction, but by design the ladder beats random on 13 of 21 designs and loses on 5 (p = 0.096); about 95 blind designs would be needed for a 95% interval below zero at the observed spread. Milestone 137 (confirmatory, flow run): on 12 more blind designs from four new families, one clock each, the ladder has 2.91% mean regret against 4.15% random and wins on 8 designs, loses on 4 (p = 0.39, so the registered primary test failed); a whole family, the integer square root, is where it loses. Pooled over 33 blind designs it wins 21 to 9 (sign p = 0.043), but the 95% interval of the mean difference (−3.26 to +0.63 points) still crosses zero; about 73 designs would be needed. Wide shifters only, one corner, global-route estimates. Milestone 143 (flow run): at a second library corner, ss_100C_1v60, the ladder beats random routing on 24 of 27 blind designs (1.96% against 6.11% regret, sign p = 0.00005), although the routed ranking between corners has a median tau-b of only 0.34 and the best sequence moves on 24 of 27 designs. Milestone 144 (flow run): at the fast corner ff_n40C_1v95 the ladder still beats random routing on 20 of 27 of the same designs (4.03% against 10.06% regret, sign p = 0.019), although the tt and ff routed rankings share almost nothing (median tau-b 0.19; the best sequence differs on all 27), and all six carry-save and dot-product designs are among its seven losses. Milestone 145 (blind flow run, 20 fresh designs at ff): the ladder loses on 3 of 10 add-chain shift amounts and 0 of 10 others (Fisher p = 0.105, so the strong reading of milestone 144 is refuted), but its edge over random routing is 7.3 points smaller on add chains (permutation p = 0.026), where the mapped rung ranks worse against routing (median tau-b 0.27 against 0.47); add-chain designs also have shorter mapped delays, a confound. Milestone 146 (blind flow run, slow add chains and fast control chains at ff): the ladder wins all 5 slow add chains and 4 of 8 fast controls; across the 2 × 2 the delay effect is +6.08 points (interval +2.58 to +9.73) and the structure effect +1.18 (−2.43 to +4.69), so the fast-corner weakness follows a short mapped critical path, not add-chain amounts. Milestone 147 (blind flow run, all four cells fresh, 20 designs): neither factor holds, add-chain effect −2.55 points (p = 0.66) and delay effect −0.09 (p = 0.99); over the 26 fresh designs of milestones 146 and 147 the delay effect is +0.01 (p = 0.997), so milestone 146's delay effect rests on milestone 145's designs. Milestone 154 (paired replay of 13 short add chains run at both ff and tt): the ladder's edge over random routing is the same at both corners (1.51 and 1.50 points); across the 26 units the edge follows how well mapped delay ranks routed delay (Spearman −0.58), not mapped area, which ranks routed area at tau-b 0.92 at both corners. Milestones 162 and 163 (netlist naming noise, 27 SKY130 ss designs): averaged over three namings of every mapped netlist the ladder's edge over random routing is −4.37 points (interval −6.56 to −2.32), and over 200 per-point naming draws a single design's edge has a median sd of 1.02 points, so per-design wins and losses larger than about 3 points survive naming noise and smaller ones are ties. Milestone 164 routed two more random namings on the six near-zero designs: a naming shared by a whole table moves a design's edge up to 3.8 points (outside two per-point sd on 5 of 12), so per-design differences under about 4 points in a one-naming table are ties; averaged over five namings all six stay within 2.1 points of zero. Milestones 166 and 167 (flow runs, 10,400 place-and-route runs) rerouted all 25 decided blind shifter designs under two fresh namings: averaged over three namings every win and loss keeps its sign, 11 wins to 1 loss at 32 gates or more in front of the shift amount (sign p 0.0063) and 5 to 8 below (p 0.58), and above the cut the ladder finds the routed-best sequence on all 11 wins under every averaged naming.
